title: Mary Anning
about: the life of Mary Anning: when and where they were born, their best-known work, discovery or invention and when, a few moments from their life such as moving, studying or a turning point, and when they died if they have. Include several specific numbers, dates or names where the topic has them, some exact and some rounded or hedged (about, nearly, more than, up to).
passages: Mary Anning was born on 21 May 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small seaside town on the south coast of England. Its crumbling cliffs hold rocks nearly 200 million years old, packed with ancient sea creatures turned to stone. Her father, a cabinetmaker, taught her to hunt the beach for these fossils to sell to visitors. After he died in 1810, the family was poor. Around 1811, her brother Joseph spotted a strange skull, and Mary, only about 12, later dug out the rest of the body. It was an ICHTHYOSAUR, a fish-shaped reptile more than 5 metres long.

In 1823 she uncovered the first complete PLESIOSAUR, a creature with a tiny head, a very long neck and four flippers. Some experts doubted it was real until they saw it for themselves. In 1828 she found a flying reptile, a PTEROSAUR, the first ever dug up outside Germany. Scientists came from across Europe to visit her little shop, yet as a woman she was not allowed to join the GEOLOGICAL Society of London. Mary died on 9 March 1847, aged 47. Today her cliffs are part of the Jurassic Coast, a World Heritage Site stretching about 150 kilometres.
